notes.21:1: Greek en tais psychais, literally "for the souls," uses the Septuagint idiom for deceased persons or corpses; unlike the singular Hebrew, the Greek uses the plural.
notes.21:4: The Greek reads exapina ("suddenly"), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads ba'al ("husband" or "chief/leader").
notes.21:8: The Greek reads third-person singular hagiasei ("he shall sanctify him") rather than second-person ("you shall sanctify him"); the unexpressed subject may be an unspecified Israelite, the Lord, or reflexive.
notes.21:10: Greek apokidarōsei specifically means "remove the turban from" (from kidaris, the priestly turban), whereas the Hebrew refers to unbinding or uncovering the head.
notes.21:20: Several Septuagint defect terms specify conditions differently from the Hebrew, including ephēlos ("having a white spot in the eye"), ptilos tous ophthalmous ("bleary in the eyes"), and monarchis ("one with only one testicle"), along with ōtotmētos ("with a cut ear") and hand before foot in 21:19.
notes.22:9: The Greek reads ean de bebēlōsousin auta ("and if they profane them") as a separate conditional clause and adds ho theos ("God") in "the Lord God who sanctifies them."
notes.22:13: The Greek reads chēra ekbeblēmenē ("a widow cast out") without a conjunction ("or"), differing from the Hebrew "a widow or a divorced woman."
notes.22:23: The Greek specifies ōtotmēton ("with a cut ear") and kolobokerkon ("with a docked tail") and permits making them sphagia ... seautō ("animals for slaughter for yourself"), whereas the Hebrew permits offering such an animal as a freewill offering.
notes.22:29: The Greek adds euchēn ("a vow") and translates the Hebrew "thanksgiving" with charmosynēs ("of joy").
notes.22:32: The Greek reads to onoma tou hagiou ("the name of the Holy One") rather than "My holy name" (cf. 22:2).
notes.23:4: The Greek reads "and these; proclaim them holy" (καὶ αὗται, ἁγίας καλέσατε αὐτάς) rather than "holy convocations which you shall proclaim" as in other manuscripts and the Hebrew Masoretic Text, likely reflecting an early scribal shift from κληταί ("convocations") to καὶ αὗται ("and these").
notes.23:11: The Greek specifies "on the day after the first day" (τῇ ἐπαύριον τῆς πρώτης), referring to the day after the first day of Unleavened Bread rather than "the day after the Sabbath" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text (compare 23:15, where the Greek retains "the Sabbath").
notes.23:15: Greek ἐπίθεμα ("placed offering," literally something laid upon; also in 23:17, 20) corresponds to what the Hebrew Masoretic Text calls a "wave offering." In 23:13 and 23:17, "two-tenths" denotes two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour, and a "hin" is a liquid measure.
notes.23:40: The Greek adds branches of "chaste tree" (ἄγνος) alongside willow from a stream, and places "of the year" (τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ) at the end of 23:40 while 23:41 omits the Hebrew Masoretic Text's opening clause about celebrating the feast for seven days in the year.
notes.23:43: The Greek reads ἴδωσιν ("may see") rather than εἰδῶσιν ("may know"), though the two forms were pronounced identically in Koine Greek.
notes.24:7: The Greek explicitly adds "and salt" (καὶ ἅλα) alongside pure frankincense on the stack of loaves, and describes them as "set forth" (προκείμενα) rather than as an offering by fire as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.24:11: The Greek renders the offense as "having named the Name" (ἐπονομάσας ... τὸ ὄνομα) and cursing rather than "blasphemed" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, reflecting Second Temple reverence against pronouncing the divine name; it also has plural "they brought them" (αὐτούς) to Moses.
notes.24:16: As in 24:11, the Greek forbids "naming" (ὀνομάζων / ὀνομάσαι) the name of the Lord rather than "blaspheming" it as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and explicitly adds "of Israel" and "of the Lord."
notes.24:21: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Greek omits the opening clause regarding restitution for killing an animal (already stated in 24:18) and retains only the clause on striking a person.
notes.25:10: Greek ἀφέσεως σημασία ("signal of release") renders the Hebrew Jubilee (yobel) with reference to the trumpet signal proclaiming the fiftieth year of release, repeated in vv. 11-13.
notes.25:27: The Greek source reads ὅπερ ἔχει ("what he has," rather than ὃ ὑπερέχει, "the remainder") and explicitly includes ἑαυτὸν ("to whom he sold himself").
notes.25:28: The Greek source distinctly reads τοῦ ἕκτου ἔτους τῆς ἀφέσεως ("the sixth year of release") and κατάπαυσιν ("rest") rather than κατάσχεσιν ("possession").
notes.25:33: The elliptical Greek construction ὃς ἂν λυτρωσάμενος παρὰ τῶν Λευειτῶν ("whoever redeems from the Levites") uses a participle with ὃς ἂν to render a notoriously debated legal clause on Levitical house redemption.
notes.25:55: The Greek text concludes with the exodus statement and does not include the closing formula "I am the Lord your God" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.26:1: The Septuagint opens with "I am the Lord your God" (absent from the Masoretic Text) and translates Hebrew even maskit ("figured stone") as lithon skopon ("lookout stone," literally a stone set as a watch-post or visual mark).
notes.26:11: The Greek text reads "My covenant" (ten diatheken mou), differing from the Masoretic Text's "My dwelling/tabernacle."
notes.26:21: Greek plagios, repeated seven times in vv. 21-41, literally means "sideways" or "oblique," expressing contrary hostility both in Israel's walk toward God and in God's responsive "sideways wrath."
notes.26:36: The Greek text reads doulian ("bondage/slavery," matching v. 45) rather than deilian ("faintness/cowardice," which corresponds to the Masoretic Text).
notes.26:41: The Greek reads apolo ("I will destroy them") rather than the Masoretic Text's "I brought them," and uses eudokesousin ("accept," literally "be well pleased with") to translate Hebrew ratsah ("accept the penalty of / make amends for").
notes.27:5: The Greek text reads "fourteen didrachmas" for a female aged five to twenty, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text (and some Greek manuscripts) reads ten.
notes.27:17: Throughout verses 17-24, the Greek renders the jubilee year as "the year of release" (aphesis), emphasizing the remission and return of property.
notes.27:19: The Greek text reads "the one who bought it" (ho agorasas), contrasting with "the one who consecrated it" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.27:23: The Greek reads "from the year of release" (ek) rather than "until the year of jubilee" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and uses telos ("total" or "full sum") for the calculated valuation.
notes.27:25: Throughout this chapter, the Greek expresses sanctuary weight standards using Greek equivalents: "didrachma" (didrachmon) for the shekel and "obols" (oboloi) for gerahs, alongside "kor" (koros) in verse 16.
